line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 Bc4 d6 Nxe5 dxe5 d3
teaches: A piece down, the temptation is to look for the refutation immediately. There usually isn't one yet. The moves that make a sacrifice work are the boring ones — hold the centre, get the king safe — because the compensation is TIME, and time is only worth something once the pieces that spend it are on the board.
explains: The modest pawn to d3 holds the pawn on e4 and opens the diagonal for the last minor piece, with the bishop on c4 already defended. Nothing is threatened and nothing needs to be: the position is being made solid before it is made sharp.

line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Nc3 Bc5 Bc4 d6 Nxe5 dxe5 d3 Qf6 O-O
teaches: An opponent who brings the queen out early to threaten mate is doing your work for you when you are behind on material. Castle: the king reaches safety, a rook joins the defence of the square being attacked, and the queen that came out to threaten now has to be spent retreating. Answer an early queen with development, never with panic.
explains: Castling puts the rook on f1 and defends the pawn on f2 the queen was eyeing. The threat is answered by a move that was needed anyway.
